title: Property and Parameter Access
description: Every supported way to read and write resource properties and step parameters.

# Property and Parameter Access

Resource **properties** and step **parameters** are stored the same way and are
read the same way. `ParameterSchema` deliberately mirrors `PropertySchema`, so
once you know one you know the other.

Writing them differs, and that difference is the main thing this page exists to
record.

```{python}
#| include: false
from pathlib import Path

Path("access-reference.db").unlink(missing_ok=True)
```

```{python}
#| include: false
from recap import RecapClient, Direction

client = RecapClient.from_sqlite("access-reference.db")
client.create_namespace("ref")
namespace = client.namespace("ref")

with namespace.build_resource_template(
    name="Plate", type_names=["container"],
) as template:
    template.add_properties({
        "dimensions": [
            {"name": "rows", "type": "int", "default": 8},
            {"name": "temperature", "type": "float", "default": 20.0, "unit": "degC"},
        ]
    })

with namespace.build_resource(name="Plate 001", template_name="Plate") as builder:
    builder.resource.properties.dimensions.rows = 16
    builder.finalize()

# A second resource left mutable, used for the write examples below.
with namespace.build_resource(name="Plate Draft", template_name="Plate") as draft:
    draft.resource.properties.dimensions.rows = 8
draft_id = draft.resource.id

with namespace.build_process_template("Measure", "1.0") as template:
    template.add_resource_slot("plate", "container", Direction.input)
    (
        template.add_step("Scan")
        .add_parameters({
            "acquisition": [
                {"name": "exposure", "type": "float", "default": 0.1, "unit": "s"},
            ]
        })
        .bind_slot("source", "plate")
        .close_step()
    )

plate = namespace.query_maker().resources().filter(name="Plate 001").first()

with namespace.build_process_run(
    name="Scan 001", description="reference run",
    template_name="Measure", version="1.0",
) as run:
    run.assign_resource("plate", plate)
    params = run.get_params("Scan")
    params.acquisition.exposure = 0.25
    run.set_params(params)
    run.finalize()

scan = (
    namespace.query_maker().process_runs().filter(name="Scan 001")
    .include_steps(include_parameters=True).first()
)
step = scan.steps["Scan"]
```

## The shape

Both follow the same four-level chain:

```text
resource.properties . <group> . <attribute> . value
step.parameters     . <group> . <attribute> . value
```

The third level is not a bare number or string. It is a small **wrapper** that
carries the value together with its unit and its template definition. The
`.value` at the end is what unwraps it.

## Reading

```{python}
print(plate.properties.dimensions.rows.value)      # a resource property
print(step.parameters.acquisition.exposure.value)  # a step parameter
```

### `.values` is optional

The wrapper models live under a `values` attribute, but both properties and
parameters forward attribute access through it, so you can leave it out. These
are equivalent:

```{python}
print(plate.properties.dimensions.rows.value)
print(plate.properties.dimensions.values.rows.value)
```

Prefer the short form. The long form is only useful when you want the values
model itself, for example to call `.keys()` on it.

### `.value` is not optional

Omitting `.value` gives you the wrapper, not the value. The wrapper renders as
its value when printed, so this mistake survives a `print()` and fails at the
first comparison:

```{python}
rows = plate.properties.dimensions.rows

print("printed:       ", rows)
print("rows == 16:    ", rows == 16)
print("rows.value:    ", rows.value)
print("rows.value==16:", rows.value == 16)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The wrapper prints like the value but is not equal to it

If a comparison, arithmetic operation, or function call behaves oddly, check
whether a `.value` is missing.
:::

### The wrapper carries the unit

This is why the wrapper exists:

```{python}
print(plate.properties.dimensions.temperature.unit)
print(step.parameters.acquisition.exposure.unit)
```

### Dotted access and bracket access

| Form | Accepts | Missing attribute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `properties.dimensions.rows` | slug only | `AttributeError` |
| `properties["dimensions"]["rows"]` | slug or original name | `KeyError` |
| `properties["dimensions"].get("rows")` | slug or original name | returns `None` |

Dotted access needs the slug, so a group named `"Sample Temperature"` is
`properties.sample_temperature`. Bracket access accepts either, which makes it
the right choice when names are not valid Python identifiers or are built at
runtime.

```{python}
group = plate.properties["dimensions"]

print(group["rows"].value)
print(group.get("rows").value)
print(group.get("not_a_real_attribute"))
```

## Writing properties

Assign the **raw value** to the attribute, inside a resource builder block.
There is no `.value` on the left-hand side:

```{python}
with namespace.build_resource(resource_id=draft_id) as builder:
    builder.resource.properties.dimensions.rows = 24
```

Reading it back confirms the change was saved. Note that a mutable resource is
not returned by queries, so it is read through a builder rather than
`query_maker()`:

```{python}
with namespace.build_resource(resource_id=draft_id) as check:
    print(check.get_model(update=True).properties.dimensions.rows.value)
```

Bracket forms work identically and accept original names:

```text
builder.resource.properties["dimensions"]["rows"] = 24
builder.resource.properties["dimensions"].values["rows"] = 24
```

The builder validates against the template and saves once, on clean exit. If
the block raises, nothing is written.

::: {.callout-important}
## Writes to an active resource are silently ignored

A resource is frozen once it becomes `ACTIVE`, and an attempted edit does
**not** raise. It simply has no effect:

```{python}
print("before:", plate.status)

with namespace.build_resource(resource_id=plate.id) as builder:
    builder.resource.properties.dimensions.rows = 9999

check = namespace.query_maker().resources().filter(name="Plate 001").first()
print("after: ", check.properties.dimensions.rows.value, "(9999 discarded)")
```

Since queries only return active resources, any resource you *found* by
querying is already frozen. To change one, copy it first, as described in
[Manage Resource Lifecycle](../how-to/manage-resource-lifecycle.qmd).
:::

## Writing parameters

Parameters are **not** written by assigning through a loaded process run. Use
`get_params()` and `set_params()` inside the `build_process_run` block:

```python
with namespace.build_process_run(...) as run:
    params = run.get_params("Scan")
    params.acquisition.exposure = 0.25
    run.set_params(params)
```

The model returned by `get_params()` holds the same wrappers, so you assign raw
values and read them back with `.value`:

```{python}
print(step.parameters.acquisition.exposure.value)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## In-place parameter edits do not persist

Assigning through a queried process run mutates only the in-memory copy. The
statement below succeeds and changes nothing in the database:

```text
scan.steps["Scan"].parameters.acquisition.exposure = 5.0   # no effect
```

`set_params()` is the only supported way to record parameter values.
:::

## Summary

| | Properties | Parameters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read | `resource.properties.<g>.<a>.value` | `step.parameters.<g>.<a>.value` |
| Unit | `....<a>.unit` | `....<a>.unit` |
| `.values` level | optional | optional |
| `.value` suffix | required | required |
| Write | assign on `builder.resource.properties` | `get_params()` / `set_params()` |
| Write window | while `MUTABLE` only | inside `build_process_run` |

```{python}
#| include: false
client.close()
Path("access-reference.db").unlink(missing_ok=True)
```
